I'm 36 years old and I've been farming our family's land in Quzhou since I finished middle school. Around here, the land is flat and the soil is good, but you only have so many mu — so everyone I know does the wheat-maize double crop. That's two harvests from the same piece of land in one year. You'd be a fool not to.

My wheat is already in the ground. I sowed it last October after the autumn rains, right on schedule, because if you miss that window the seedlings won't survive winter. I used an improved variety — the county extension office hands out leaflets every year, and I've had good luck with the semi-dwarf wheat types. Before sowing I ran the rotary tiller to break up the maize stubble and level the field. Now that spring has come and the wheat is greening up, I need to manage it through to harvest in early June. I'll irrigate three times: once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain-filling if the rain doesn't come. I topdressed with urea at green-up and I'll put more down at jointing — altogether about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus the compound fertilizer I put down at sowing. For chemicals, I'll spray herbicide in spring when the weeds sprout, and I'll keep an eye out for aphids and powdery mildew; if they show up, I'll spray fungicide and insecticide. I expect about 950 kg per mu from the wheat if the weather holds.

As soon as the wheat comes off in June, I have maybe three to five days to get the maize in — the summer season is short and you can't waste a single day. I'll plant a hybrid maize variety, something like what the seed dealer recommended last year. I won't till the land — I'll plant no-tillage straight into the wheat stubble. No-tillage saves diesel, keeps moisture in the ground, and more importantly saves time when every hour counts. The maize will need about 16 kg nitrogen per mu, mostly as compound fertilizer drilled in at planting and urea at the big-flare stage. I'll irrigate twice in summer if the rains fail. For pests, herbicide at planting and two more sprays for corn borers and other insects. Good hybrids on this soil can give me 1,200 kg per mu.

I thought about switching some land to cotton or watermelons like a few people in the village tried, but those prices bounce around too much and I don't have the labor for picking cotton or the setup for vegetables. Wheat and maize are safe — the grain buyer always shows up, I can sell easily, and the straw feeds my livestock. That's why I stick with what I know.
